title: Greedy Best-First in Lisbon: Fast… until it fails ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First chase the lowest heuristic on a real map-style grid in Lisbon (Alfama). In this Greedy vs A* comparison, you’ll see exactly when “fast” turns into detours.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — Why it rushes to the destination (⚡) and when it breaks.

In Greedy Best-First, the frontier priority is ONLY h(n): the estimated distance from a node to the goal. That means it can look brilliant immediately—zooming toward the target like a GPS with tunnel vision—yet still produce a longer path when the heuristic misleads.

How it chooses: it always expands the node with the smallest h(n), ignoring g(n) (cost so far). When obstacles/constraints create “heuristic traps,” Greedy may commit to a promising-looking route that later forces backtracking.

Takeaway: Greedy Best-First is fast for goal-directed exploration, but it’s not guaranteed optimal—A* wins when you need the shortest path (because it balances g(n)+h(n)).

Debate question: In your world—maps, games, robotics—which matters more: blazing speed or guaranteed shortest paths?
